Cyberbeast / Source: Tesla.com
Tesla has officially cancelled the Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand. Reservation holders are getting emails today telling them their orders are void and their deposits will be refunded.
Australians started putting down A$150 to reserve the electric pickup in November 2019. That’s almost seven years of waiting for a truck Tesla now says it won’t build for them.
“Plans… have been discontinued”
The email, which reservation holders started sharing on social media and Reddit this morning, is short.
“After careful consideration, plans to produce Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand have been discontinued,” Tesla wrote. “As a result, we’re unable to fulfil your reservation and it will be cancelled.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Tesla says customers will get a full refund for any payments made, with refunds processed within 30 days. As a consolation, the automaker is offering a free one-year subscription to FSD (Supervised) to reservation holders who order a new Model 3 or Model Y instead.
Tesla is trying to convert a dead Cybertruck reservation into a sale of a car it actually builds in right-hand drive.
The emails went out a day after Tesla reported its Q3 2026 earnings.
Seven years of “next year”
Australia wasn’t a small market on paper. A crowdsourced survey of reservations from 2020 put it third behind the US and Canada, with about 3% of all Cybertruck reservations. Tesla never confirmed regional numbers, but by 2023, crowdsourced tracking put total Cybertruck reservations at around 2 million .
Tesla quietly closed the Australian reservation page in May 2022 and replaced it with a “Get updates” button. It didn’t refund anyone at the time. People who had already reserved just kept waiting.
Then in 2024, Tesla shipped a Cybertruck down under for a display tour, and Elon Musk told shareholders that year: “We might be able to certify it for other markets sometime next year.” Next year came and went, and the truck never got a right-hand-drive version.
That’s the core problem. The Cybertruck is built only in left-hand drive. Australia, New Zealand, the UK, and Japan all need right-hand drive, and Australia also requires certification under its own design rules. That’s a big bill for a truck with a truck that is already having demand issues in North America.
The Cybertruck can’t justify the investment
Tesla’s few international Cybertruck launches all share one thing: they’re left-hand-drive markets. Deliveries started in South Korea late last year and in the UAE in January , followed by configurators in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, and Israel. The truck remains blocked in the EU, mainly for pedestrian safety reasons.
And the volumes don’t support a right-hand-drive program. Tesla delivered just 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3 2026, a category that’s now almost entirely Cybertruck since Model S and Model X production ended. We estimate Cybertruck sales at 7,000 to 8,000 units last quarter , roughly a 30,000-per-year pace for a production line Tesla built for 250,000 units annually.
At that rate, no CFO would sign off on re-engineering the truck for two markets that together have about 33 million people.
Electrek’s Take
This was the obvious outcome for a while, and Tesla should have said so years ago.
Taking deposits in 2019 for a truck that was supposed to start at $39,900 was one thing. Closing the order page in 2022 and letting thousands of people sit on refundable deposits for four more years without a word, while the CEO kept dangling “next year,” is another.
To be fair, a lot of Australian reservation holders likely already canceled their pre-orders. The Cybertruck that showed up in 2023 isn’t the one they reserved. It’s more expensive, has less range than promised, and its US sales have collapsed from about 39,000 in 2024 to a fraction of that today. Paying a premium for an import-ready version would have made it even worse value down under.
But it also confirms what we’ve been saying: the Cybertruck is now a niche, mostly American product. Tesla isn’t likely to invest more in it, and the international expansion is just about finding buyers for the existing left-hand-drive trucks.

source_document.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the power requirements of modern data centers. At this point in the timeline of AI’s continued evolution, this statement should not be controversial. The deployment of increasingly large GPU clusters for training and inference purposes, such as NVIDIA’s 72-GPU Vera Rubin model , is causing rack power densities to climb from tens to hundreds of kilowatts (kW), with some next-generation designs projected to exceed one megawatt (MW) per rack.
This creates much more power demand than traditional enterprise computing infrastructure was designed to support. Workloads that behave very differently than conventional applications are forcing operators to reevaluate their long-standing assumptions about power delivery and efficiency. What were once straightforward design decisions have become more complex in the face of unpredictable power densities and utilization patterns.
One such assumption concerns the role of efficiency in power system design. For years, developers have been focused on designing systems for peak efficiency, where systems operate optimally under truly ideal conditions. But as evolving AI workloads inject uncertainty into the equation, developers must reconsider whether these traditional efficiency-based models accurately reflect how data center infrastructure actually operates—or if they’re designing around unrealistic “ideal” standards.
The answer has implications that extend beyond energy consumption to cooling requirements, material usage, infrastructure costs, and data centers’ overall ability to scale alongside AI demand.
AI Has Rewritten the Power Delivery Playbook
The power architectures used in many of today’s data centers were largely developed around predictable computing workloads. Traditional enterprise applications, web hosting environments, and business systems all tend to operate within relatively stable utilization ranges, which means power infrastructure could be optimized around expected load. AI workloads, however, behave quite differently than their steadier predecessors.
Large-scale AI training work relies on thousands of GPUs operating in parallel, often processing data in synchronized bursts. Utilization fluctuates rapidly during these training cycles, and can swing from roughly 30% utilization to full utilization in milliseconds as GPUs move between computation, communication, and memory-access operations. These shifts generate significant fluctuations in power demand across servers, racks, and even entire data center facilities—and they only become more pronounced as rack densities increase.
This combination of high power density and dynamic load behavior creates challenges that span the entire power chain. Power supplies, converters, distribution equipment, and cooling systems must all respond to rapid changes in demand while maintaining stable operation. As a result, developers must adopt a fundamental shift in the ways they evaluate and design power systems for data centers. The challenge isn’t to simply deliver more power, but to do so efficiently and reliably across fluctuating operating conditions.
Why Peak Efficiency Can Be a Misleading Target
Historically, power conversion systems have been designed and evaluated around the concept of peak efficiency, or the maximum efficiency achieved at a specific operating point. This approach provided a useful benchmark for relatively stable workloads, as peak efficiency could offer a pretty reasonable indication of the system’s real-world performance.
The same cannot be said for today’s evolving AI workloads. Their training and inference processes cause utilization to fluctuate dramatically, rarely leaving systems in any single, steady-state condition. Rather, they move through a range of load levels and often spend more time operating at partial loads than under peak efficiency conditions.
This is an important distinction to make, as efficiency curves are very rarely flat. Many power conversion systems achieve their highest efficiency within a relatively narrow operating window, with performance declining as loads move either above or below that specific range. While this difference may sound minor, even a one- or two-percentage-point drop in efficiency can translate into substantial energy losses when deployed across hundreds or even thousands of GPU racks.
These losses affect more than just energy consumption: wasted power becomes heat, which in turn increases both cooling requirements and operational costs across the data center. The higher rack densities climb, the greater the consequences of this inefficiency become.
To address this challenge, developers are beginning to place greater emphasis on efficiency across the full operating range of power systems, rather than at a single peak operating point. For AI workloads, consistently high performance at mid-load conditions may be a more meaningful measure of efficiency than the peak value.
Traditional Architectures Struggle to Scale
Another core challenge in modern data center infrastructure is related to the boundaries of traditional hardware infrastructure. As AI workloads increase, they expose the physical limitations of many data centers’ legacy rack power architectures, which were designed to distribute power at relatively low voltages.
Legacy architecture, traditionally rooted in a 48 to 54-volt (V) DC busbar with further conversion at the server level, has been more than effective for supporting conventional computing workloads. But as rack power requirements grow, 54 VDC models are no longer adequate. The reason is straightforward: lower voltages require higher currents to deliver the same amount of power. As rack densities push toward hundreds of kW and beyond, current levels rise dramatically. This leads to increases in resistive losses throughout the distribution system, requiring operators to deploy larger bus bars, extra cabling, and more robust connectors—all of which increase material costs, reduce available space, and make thermal management more difficult.
Rack-level limitations only become more pronounced at megawatt-scale designs. According to some industry projections, a 1 MW rack operating with a 48 to 54V architecture will require roughly 200 kilograms (kg) of copper for adequate power distribution. The costs—both financial and spatial—of these racks grow exponentially as their capacity expands. Ultimately, operators must find a way to mitigate these costs while maintaining efficiency and supporting greater power density.
Pairing High-Voltage Distribution With Flat-Load Efficiency
To address the joint challenges of uncertain workloads and increased power density, data center operators are beginning to consider two complementary strategies:
Adopting higher-voltage power distribution architectures.
Maintaining flatter efficiency profiles.
The case for higher-voltage distribution is pretty simple. Delivering more power to racks at higher voltages reduces the amount of current flowing through the system, helping alleviate many of the limitations of low-voltage architectures. Rather than relying on traditional 48 to 54V architectures, data centers can implement ±400V or 800V DC models that reduce copper requirements, lower resistive losses, and support much higher rack-level power densities.
While higher voltages address part of the density challenge, power must still be converted and delivered efficiently across fluctuating workloads. This is where flat-load efficiency becomes crucial. Rather than optimizing performance around a single “peak” operating point, designers must focus on maintaining high efficiency across the load ranges where AI workloads actually operate. By shifting from a peak-centric model to a flat, high-load efficiency one, developers can help ensure:
Reduced energy losses during fluctuating workloads.
Lower heat generation and cooling demand.
More predictable power-system performance as utilization rates change.
Improved ability to scale as rack power levels continue to rise.
These approaches are most effective when implemented in tandem. Higher-voltage architectures help address the challenge of delivering ever-increasing amounts of power to AI data center infrastructure, while flat-efficiency power conversion helps ensure that power is being used effectively across the standard operating conditions of AI workloads.
It’s important to note that neither approach is without its own trade-offs. High-voltage racks introduce new requirements for safety, insulation, connections, and facility design, and retrofitting existing data center infrastructure can be expensive and complex. Still, as AI workloads continue to push power demands higher, it’s even more crucial that developers consider these kinds of new approaches to power distribution and efficiency.
Designing for the Real World
The assumptions we’ve long held around data center power delivery and efficiency no longer hold true in the face of AI. Between workloads characterized by rapid utilization swings and steadily increasing rack power densities, AI workloads do not operate under the same stable conditions that shaped much of today’s power architecture models. And as a result, former metrics and design considerations are becoming less-effective indicators of real-world performance.
While peak efficiency will remain an important benchmark, it’s no longer sufficient on its own. Maintaining consistent high efficiency in the flat load range of AI workloads will have a greater impact on energy consumption, thermal management needs, operating costs, and long-term scalability than achieving the highest possible efficiency at a peak operating point.
At the same time, low-voltage distribution architectures are not capable of supporting today’s growing rack densities. Adopting higher-voltage models helps forge a path that accounts for future AI infrastructure while reducing current losses and material demands. When combined, these architectural and efficiency models represent a greater shift toward designing power systems for how AI actually behaves, rather than how it’s expected to behave under ideal conditions.
— Philip Zuk is senior vice president and general manager, AI and Datacenter, with OmniOn Power .

Nothing could be further from the truth, with the American space agency attacking lunar exploration plans on all fronts.
Not long ago, in the spring of this year, NASA made public the fact that it's no longer going to the Moon on short visits, but plans to build a permanent base there. Called in the simplest fashion possible Moon Base, the future outpost seems to be getting more real every single day.
To get it up and running, but also to support the operations that will be conducted there, the Moon Base will require a lot of assistance, including from crewed and robotic lunar rovers. There are many of them being planned, both government-backed and backed by private laboratories, and it is getting quite difficult to keep track of them all.
Luckily, this week NASA gave the world an update on how things are going with the first three of them, arguably the most important of them all: the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER), the Crewed Lunar Vehicle 1 (CLV-1), and the Pegasus.
VIPER The VIPER rover has been in the news a lot in recent years, as one of NASA's most ambitious projects of this kind, and at the same time a victim of budget cuts. Through a stroke of luck, the rover will get to launch to the lunar South Pole next year on board a Blue Origin Blue Moon Mark 1 lander.
Photo: NASA Tasked with looking for water and other valuable resources, the machine will have to travel a total distance of 18 miles (30 km) to fulfill its mission objectives. Presently, the VIPER is being prepped for launch at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, and will soon move to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
CLV-1 Back in the spring of this year, the agency settled on the two rovers that will advance the human exploration of the Moon. The Astrolab-made Crewed Lunar Vehicle 1 (CLV-1) is one of the two, derived from the company's previous Flexible Logistics and Exploration Vehicle (FLEX).
The origin story of this rover is a bit more complicated, as it won't be sent directly to the Moon in the final configuration. Another version of it, called the FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP), will travel up there on board Voyager Technologies’ Griffin Mission One, scheduled to launch later this year. The lessons learned with this smaller version will be implemented in the full-size CLV-1.
As you're reading this, a mockup of the CLV-1 has been delivered to Axiom Space to be evaluated by Artemis astronauts dressed in mockups of the upcoming space suits. Separately, the rover's innovative, airless wheels will be put through their paces at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio.
Pegasus Photo: NASA Put together by Lunar Outpost and derived from a previous design called Eagle, the Pegasus lunar terrain vehicle (LTV) has already been tested in a way on the Moon, using the Mobile Autonomous Prospecting Platform (MAPP) rover the company sent to the satellite in 2025. A second MAPP is scheduled to be sent up there early next year.
A total of three Pegasus mockups have already been built, and one of them is being put through its paces at the Johnson Space Center, including in the hands of suited astronauts.
Both crew-rated rovers are set to be sent to the Moon by 2028. The first examples will be remote-controlled from Earth, and they are expected to cover some 3.7 miles (six km) per day, mapping the region and snapping images of it.
When the time comes, in subsequent crewed Artemis missions, astronauts will climb on board and drive the rovers around, exploring various points of interest at the South Pole. As per the program's requirements, each rover will have to be able to support up to three moonwalks per Artemis mission.
Photo: NASA When it comes to capabilities, each of them needs to be able to carry up to 176 pounds (80 kg) of lunar material and tools, and cover up to six miles (ten km) on a single charge of the battery. To make sure the designs fulfill those requirements, both Astrolab and Lunar Outpost will test drivable LTV mockups with NASA crews in the coming weeks, in an undisclosed, simulated lunar environment.
NASA has plans to complete the preliminary design review of both LTVs by the end of this month, with the complete designs expected to be delivered at the end of next year.
Needless to say, the upcoming Moon Base will require much more than a single pack of rovers. NASA plans three main missions in the near term to start building it. Moon Base 1, scheduled for the fall of this year, also happens to be the mission that will get the VIPER to its destination.
Then, Moon Base II, scheduled for later this year, will deliver the Astrolab FLIP, among other things, while Moon Base III will send to the Moon the Intuitive Machines Nova-C Trinity lunar lander.

A new proposal from the U.S. government seeking to address investment in Chinese biotech as a matter of national security drew cautious statements from across the industry, with leaders vowing to ensure innovation isn’t stifled.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has taken steps to restrict outbound biotechnology investments to protect national security, acting on direction from President Donald Trump.
The proposal seeks to restrict U.S. persons from investing in certain bio-derived compounds, biomanufacturing equipment and facilities, biotechnology or equipment involved in biological design and scientific discovery or experimentation.
But licensing deals would not be off limits, according to a fact sheet that accompanied the proposal, leaving pharmaceutical companies open to continue transacting in China as they have increasingly been for the past few years.
The Treasury Department’s proposal comes a week after China similarly rolled out a new policy to restrict the transfer of ownership for certain biotechnologies, including cell and gene therapy—while also exempting licensing deals .
China
China’s licensing deals soar as US biotechs enjoy a bumper M&A year
China may be taking the majority of licensing deals this year but those transactions don’t tell the whole story, according to Locust Walk, which points to the spike in M&A among U.S. biotechs as leveling the playing field.

The new U.S. proposal drew cautious statements from across the industry, with leaders vowing to carefully review the fine print and ensure that innovation isn’t stifled.
“We need policies and initiatives that maintain and advance our global leadership in biotech, particularly as we compete with China,” John Crowley, CEO of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), said in a Thursday statement . “The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter. We cannot restrict our way to success.”
Crowley has been an outspoken voice on the rising dominance of China’s biotech sector, warning of national security risks and the need to boost U.S. companies. In response to the official proposal, Crowley urged the U.S. government to ensure that the new rules do not unintentionally weaken U.S. biotechs.
The proposal comes from the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act, which was passed by Congress in the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. Trump signed the COINS Act into law in December 2025.
The proposal focused heavily on brain-computer interface technology but more broadly suggested naming the following as prohibited technologies from countries of concern: small molecules, polymers, vaccines, blood and blood components, allergenics, cell and gene therapies, and monoclonal antibodies or other recombinant therapeutic proteins.
“It is necessary to place restrictions in this sector in the interest of protecting U.S. national security,” the rule states; “at the same time, the Treasury Department recognizes that restrictions may potentially have countervailing effects on national security to the extent restrictions lead to significant public health risks or harm U.S. businesses in this sector.”
The department is therefore seeking comment on the possible risks of restrictions and the impact on national security.
“The proposed regulations are designed to address risks that can arise when foreign adversaries try to benefit from U.S. investment in key technology sectors,” Christopher Pilkerton, assistant secretary of the Treasury for Investment Security, said in a statement .
While industry leaders have been calling for a more committed strategy from the U.S. to support homegrown biotechs, they have stopped short of calling for a ban on licensing deals.
Deals
China tightens grip on biotech platform ownership but foreign licensing deals still okay
The new policy signals an escalation by the Chinese government on biopharma deals but is unlikely to have a major impact given that the vast majority of foreign interest in Chinese biotech comes in the form of licensing agreements.
October 19, 2026

“We are in a new space race,” said Patroski Lawson, founder of the KPM Group and the American Biotech Innovation Alliance, during a BioSpace webinar on the rise of China biotech earlier this month. “Patients don’t care. Patients just want innovation, right? So it’s incumbent upon us to be thinking more strategically rather than in sort of this fragmented ad hoc approach that we’ve taken to this.
“China is gaining on us,” he continued. “We’re not sure exactly how much they’re catching up, and what are we going to do about it? Are we going to continue complaining, or are we going to get our act together?”
Meanwhile, with China and the U.S. trading potentially restricting policy proposals, Sidley Partner Lila Hope said the back-and-forth is injecting uncertainty into the dealmaking process. This could push Chinese biotechs to instead look to Europe, Japan or other areas for deals.
“We’re not helping ourselves by turning away from this,” Hope said on the BioSpace webinar. “What we ought to do is try to see what are the opportunities to collaborate. You have good asset. I have talent. Let’s bring it here and develop it together.”

This Guy Has Been Working for Ford for 60 Years, Has Tools Older Than His Workmates
8 photos
Photo: Ford From the Road
The first time Eddie O'Brien walked through the gates of the Ford Dagenham plant, back in 1966, he was a 16-year-old apprentice. Fast forward to 2026, and he has just celebrated 60 years with the company with no interruption whatsoever.
Eddie O'Brien has been with Ford through 13 different Prime Ministers. Back when he started, England had just won the World Cup, something it has not done again since. The world has changed over the years, but one thing has remained the same. Eddie showed up for his shift, day or night.
His own celebration in 2026 coincides with a major anniversary for his workplace. The event that marked his six-decade-long career with Ford took place exactly 95 years after the Ford Dagenham site started operating.
Dagenham is now a major powertrain hub, producing high-volume diesel engines, such as the 2.0-liter EcoBlue, for Ford’s global commercial vehicle lineup. But for 71 years, the manufacturing facility was a massive vehicle assembly facility, rolling out over 11 million cars, trucks, and tractors, including models such as the Cortina , Capri, and Fiesta. Vehicle assembly officially ceased at the site in 2002, when the final UK-built Ford Fiesta rolled off the production line.
Photo: Ford From the Road For him, the Blue Oval adventure started with the Ford Trade School, doing what they called a sandwich course. At the time, he actually applied for three jobs. One was at a rubber factory in Essex, and another was with British Gas. But he wanted to work for Ford the most, so here he is, 60 years later.
He began training at the specialized company trade school located in nearby Harold Hill. Upon entering the main Dagenham complex, he was first deployed to the River Plant. He later transitioned to the facility’s Central Repair Garage to sharpen his mechanical expertise.
In 1973, he found his permanent home within the company. For over five decades, he has worked specifically as a Mechanical Maintenance Craftsman. His primary responsibility has been maintaining the massive infrastructure required to handle vehicle logistics, keeping heavy industrial machinery, site tugs, and locomotives running smoothly.
Many refer to the machine shop where he spends most of his time as "Eddie's Shop." It is where he does his job and has tools older than some of his current workmates. He bought them himself ages ago. He remembers that he paid 5 pounds for a micrometer to gauge small distances and thickness. That was a week’s wages at the time. He remembers he and his colleagues were paid in cash back then.
Photo: Ford From the Road There are photos of him in black and white up on the walls, showing different stages of his career. Eddie credits his incredible work longevity in a demanding blue-collar career to his lifetime dedication to physical health, particularly his love for cycling and taking part in charity bike rides. He took up cycling about 24 years ago and hasn't stopped since.
He only wished he'd started sooner. If he had, he would have ridden more than the few 100-mile races that he has completed so far. He still does it, usually in the company of one of his sons outdoors or by himself, indoors. " I do like to push it, get my blood pumping ," he says.
He also takes his grandchildren cycling every once in a while. Staying active is probably one of the reasons he hasn't gained weight over the years. He also took up running ten years ago but had to stop after he injured his foot.
He is well aware that now, his time at Ford is inching closer to the end due to the physical demands of the job and admits that " 60 years is a nice number to sign off on ." " I think some of the younger guys do look after me a little bit. Not too much, " he says.
Photo: Ford From the Road The best part of his job? He got to work on and for some iconic vehicles. For instance, he had to make jigs for some repairs for the Le Mans Ford GT40 at the Heritage Center as fast as he could because they needed them for a TV show. As a reward, he received a plaque with one of the pistons from the blow-up engine on it.
He has been a Ford owner over all these years. He drives a Fiesta now, but he has had Cortinas, other Fiestas, and even Transits, along with a Sierra, which he affectionately calls his favorite. However, he has always been in love with motorcycles. He has even raced them until 1988. He has recently sold his Kawasaki 500 Enduro that he used to ride to work every day, regardless of the weather. All of a sudden, he no longer enjoyed it, so he got rid of it.
Once he retires, he plans to focus on cycling and spending time with his family, especially with his grandchildren and great-grandchildren. He wasn't even planning to start a family in the near future when he started working for Ford.

By Raymon Krishnan, president, The Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society
23 October 2026
Dropping behind Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan in the global container port rankings, and seeing Malaysia’s Port Klang and Port of Tanjung Pelepas nip at its heels should serve as a wake-up call for Singapore, in a changing competitive landscape for box trades
For Singapore, this is about more than losing a place in a league table. It is an existential question asking whether a nation built on maritime trade can adapt to a world where supply chain control matters as much as moving containers.
As Singapore spent years living off its geographical advantages, deepwater harbour and reputation for efficiency to guarantee continued dominance, its competitors have expanded their infrastructure, attracted manufacturing investment, and developed integrated logistics ecosystems. The danger now for Singapore is that it continues competing on volumes, while the market moves towards supply chain orchestration.
How do the two differ? A transit port moves containers; a supply chain orchestrator helps determine where goods are sourced, stored, distributed, and financed, allowing it to capture greater economic value, even if cargo physically passes through another country.
Part of the problem for Singapore with its nearest rival is that it simply cannot compete with Malaysia when it comes to land availability, meaning it should not focus on warehouses and distribution centres. Instead, it should tap into the long-held advantages it has in expertise, connectivity, technology, and managing complex regional supply chains.
That means attracting multinational manufacturers, cargo owners, and third-party logistics providers, particularly those active in high-value sectors such as biopharma, semiconductors, and aerospace spares, thereby building on the island’s existing strengths. And the objective should be keeping procurement, inventory management, supply chain finance, and regional logistics decisions in Singapore, even if the boxes end up elsewhere.
All of this necessitates closer integration between sea, air, and land transport, back-up by digital systems giving businesses greater visibility and control. And if Singapore’s transport infrastructure operates as a connected ecosystem, its compact geography could prove a further significant advantage.
And the pending Tuas Port, with its planned capacity of 65m teu on full completion in the 2040s, will have a part to play, even if success cannot be judged by volume alone. With nearshoring, manufacturing diversification, and geopolitical disruption reshaping trade, uninterrupted container growth cannot be taken for granted. For this reason, Tuas should, instead, provide resilience, operational flexibility, and capacity to absorb sudden changes in trade flows. Investment in alternative marine fuels and emissions data could also attract shippers facing tougher sustainability requirements.
But again, infrastructure is only half the equation. No commercially ambitious ecosystem? Then even the most automated port risks becoming little more than an efficient place to park containers.
Government has a role to play in this. Yes, the Ministry of Transport’s new Connectivity & Logistics division recognises the need to integrate maritime, aviation, and land transport, but creating a coordinating body will not automatically deliver the commercial agility needed to compete. Instead, the government must work to embed industry expertise in its strategy. Consultations have their place, but they cannot replace the practical intelligence of logistics providers, cargo owners, and technology companies. These businesses understand rising costs, unreliable corridors, and customers’ needs. They should help develop and execute strategy, not simply comment on government proposals.
Singapore’s position is under pressure, but its future as a supply chain powerhouse is far from decided. In 1972, Singapore made a bold bet on containerisation by developing Tanjong Pagar. The infrastructure, expertise, and connectivity that emerged from that remain valuable assets. The challenge now is to turn them into a more ambitious commercial proposition.
If ’72 brought containerisation, ’26 requires a similarly decisive shift: from moving boxes to orchestrating supply chains.

NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan— China’s first aircraft carrier, heavily watched around East Asia as an emblem of Beijing’s growing naval power , had made at least six faraway deployments since its completion 14 years ago.
It made another in October.
So frequent are the Chinese aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning’s publicly visible voyages that military analysts presume that the People’s Liberation Army Navy has fixed a routine that will let the relatively aged carrier help train and equip the fleet’s two more modern ones.
Still, the carrier group’s passages not far from Taiwan , Japan and the Philippines – places that have political or maritime sovereignty disputes with China – have raised alerts .
“The current voyage by the Liaoning appears to be part of an established evolving pattern of far-seas training deployments,” said Carl Thayer, an Asia specialist and emeritus professor at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
“The Liaoning demonstrates China’s naval military capability and political influence through its constant presence in China’s near and far seas,” he said.
The aircraft carrier led a naval task group to the western Pacific Ocean on Oct. 14 for training, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy said via China’s official Xinhua News Agency. Citing the navy, Xinhua called the expedition a “drill” and part of an annual routine training plan aimed at “testing and improving combat readiness.”
China’s state-controlled Global Times news outlet called the Liaoning’s October voyage its second in the distant seas and hailed the carrier’s long-term progress as going from a “coastal pathfinder” to a “far-sea blade.”
The vessel, categorized as a “short take-off but arrested recovery” aircraft carrier, measures about 305 meters (1,000 feet) long and with flight deck width up to 75 meters.
As of Oct. 23, the carrier group had done exercises near the southernmost Japanese outlying islands and was headed for the South China Sea near the Philippines, according to local media reports in East Asia. The reports said it went with two large destroyers and a guided-missile destroyer.
The deployments are meant to show China’s two more-modern carriers, the CNS Fujian and the CNS Shandong, how to adopt new technology, experts said.
The nine-year-old Shandong carrier would learn about “new and emerging” technology as the older Liaoning tests flight operations, sensors and modern aircraft, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
“The Shandong aircraft carrier is basically an improved version of the Liaoning,” Koh said. He said the current deployment was probably “meant maybe to validate certain technologies.”
Being the oldest of China’s three carriers, the Liaoning would “not be the frontline reaction force if there were a contingency”, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.
China’s maritime rivals have taken notice.
The Taiwan Ministry of National Defense said in mid-October it was monitoring the possibility of large-scale Chinese military exercises nearby as an outcome of the Liaoning’s movements.
China claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to take it. The PLA has stepped up military activity in waters near the island since 2022.
In the South China Sea, Beijing has already shored up its sovereignty claims over the past two decades by building artificial islands, often for military use. Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam dispute parts of the sea with China.
In Tokyo, which disputes a group of uninhabited islets with Beijing, the defense ministry said it had seen fighter aircraft taking off and landing from the Liaoning carrier 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Japan’s Ishigaki Island.
The Chinese carrier group launched and recovered aircraft in Japan’s maritime exclusive economic zone during its deployment, said Colin Karotam, senior resident fellow with the Defence Strategy Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. That activity is “uncommon,” Karotam said, though it may have taken place before.
The Chinese carrier group’s activities also began shortly before the Keen Sword 27 U.S.–Japan military exercises launched on Oct. 19. The exercises on Ishigaki are biennial and include the Philippines among other nations. China sees the United States, a treaty ally of both Japan and the Philippines, as a military rival in Asia.
Xinhua said the Liaoning’s movements in October comply with international law and “are not directed at any specific country or target.”

Sixteen Massachusetts lawmakers are asking Gov. Maura Healey to freeze state approvals for commercial drone delivery as Amazon seeks to launch Prime Air service from its Westborough warehouse .
What’s Related
In an Oct. 19 letter, the bipartisan group requested a task force to review the state’s drone delivery rules and recommend changes. They also want state agencies to stop accepting or processing applications for commercial drone delivery certificates until that work is complete.
According to Sen. Michael Moore’s office, residents have raised concerns about noise, flight routes, operating hours, safety , privacy, cybersecurity and environmental impacts. Although Amazon’s proposal prompted the letter, the requested freeze would apply to all commercial drone delivery operators.
Healey’s office says it is reviewing the request. A statewide freeze has not been announced.
“We are evaluating our options to make sure that the community’s interests are protected,” Healey spokesperson Jacqui Manning told State House News Service.
RELATED STORIES: Prime Air Expands Drone Delivery to Nearly 500 Cities | Amazon Launches Prime Air Drone Deliveries in the UK
Amazon faces state review
Amazon plans to deliver packages weighing less than 5 pounds within a 7.5-mile radius of its Westborough fulfillment center. According to Moore’s office, the company hopes to eventually make up to 1,000 deliveries a day from the site.
In an Oct. 22 letter , MassDOT Administrator Denise Garcia told Amazon it must obtain state approval before establishing a drone takeoff and landing area. The agency said it had not received an official request from Amazon for review.
Phil Eng, MassDOT’s interim secretary, said the agency will hold a public hearing so residents have “a meaningful opportunity to be heard.”
That review is separate from the proposed statewide freeze. While the Federal Aviation Administration oversees airspace, the lawmakers argue Massachusetts should use its authority over takeoff and landing sites to plan where drone delivery hubs can go.
Westborough challenges Amazon’s drone plans
Westborough residents voted 510-13 at an Oct. 19 Special Town Meeting to approve a bylaw restricting commercial drone ground activity. It includes a 150-foot buffer between drone staging areas and employee parking, workplace entrances and pedestrian walkways.
The bylaw requires approval from the Attorney General and MassDOT’s Aeronautics Division before taking effect.
On Nov. 2, the town’s Zoning Board of Appeals will hear an appeal of the code enforcement officer’s ruling that drone delivery is allowed at the site. If the board overturns that ruling, Amazon would need to apply for a special permit.
Amazon told State House News Service it knows an appeal has been filed over the town’s zoning interpretation and is working through the process with local officials and surrounding communities.
Rep. Kate Donaghue, whose district includes Westborough, said drone delivery “has the potential for expansion far beyond this specific site and this specific vendor.” She questioned whether current rules adequately address shared airspace, commercial activity, and delivery services growing in size.
“I am hopeful that a task force can shed light on these questions and lead to positive outcomes for our residents,” she said.

By Gavin van Marle
23 October 2026
Container spot freight rates on all three of the largest east-west trades – Asia-Europe, transpacific, and transatlantic – were on the rise this week.
After three months of post-peak season declines, the Asia-Europe trades experienced a second week of spot freight rate increases, according to Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI).
The WCI’s Shanghai-Rotterdam leg was up 3% week on week, to end at to $3,632 per 40ft, while its Shanghai-Genoa route saw pricing increase 5%, to $4,152 per 40ft.
As is often the case, this week’s WCI Asia-Europe spot rate levels were indicated by last week’s Shanghai Containerised Freight Index (SCFI) figures, which showed Shanghai-North Europe at $3,547 per 40ft, and Shanghai-Mediterranean at $4,097 per 40ft, while analysts at Linerlytica noted that “actual spot rates remain weak with current carrier rates at below the SCFI’s assessment”, which chimes with some of the unsolicited spot market offers The Loadstar received from Chinese forwarders this week.
In an effort to stave off a downturn in pricing as the market moves into November, carriers are increasing the number of blanked sailings – according to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, eight blank sailings have been announced for next week, up from two this week, “indicating tight capacity”, as well as introducing new freight all kinds (FAK) prices on Asia-Europe.
This week MSC announced it would apply an FAK of $4,500 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe, $5,000 on Asia-west Mediterranean, and $5,100 on Asia-east Mediterranean on 1 November, while CMA CGM is aiming for $4,900 on Asia-west Mediterranean and $5,200 on Asia-east Mediterranean ports for the same date.
However, Linerlytica predicts the new November pricing will likely fail, although it is worth noting that in MSC’s case, the FAK rate to North Europe is the same level as that introduced in mid-October and only $500 per 40ft up in terms of Mediterranean destinations.
European forwarders reported receiving discounted offers on FAK levels throughout the first half of this month and suggested this will be repeated in November.
Meanwhile, transpacific spot rates grew more modestly in a week which US west coast forwarder Freight Right described as “a market stabilising”.
The WCI’s Shanghai-Los Angeles leg rose 2% week on week, to finish at $8,007 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-New route was York up 1%, to $10,166 per 40ft, with Drewry recording two blank sailings scheduled for next week, “down from six this week, indicating more effective capacity”.
“Since strong US import demand continues to support freight rates, Drewry expects rates to remain stable next week,” the consultancy added.
However, North American demand levels remain open to question, with Freight Right reporting that a much-anticipated seasonal slowdown was beginning with the peak shipping season “officially wrapping up, and volume is beginning a natural seasonal decline”, combining with a modest injection of capacity and some carriers offering discounts to gain market share.
“While baseline market rates remain flat through month-end, additional capacity is opening up,” it said.
“Aggressive pricing anomalies exist among niche carriers, such as Ocean Network Express (ONE), offering rates significantly below general market averages, though space on these lower-cost options is fully booked through October,” it added.
It further added that a spot rate of around $8,000 per 40ft was now common on the Asia-US east coast trade.
“Space conditions have eased in tandem with the west coast, ending the extreme tightness observed earlier in the season,” it said.
Meanwhile, rates on the transatlantic westbound head-haul grew again this week, with the WCI’s Rotterdam-New York showing 3% week-on-week increases, to end at $3,181 per 40ft, maintaining a a months-long run that has seen the spot rate persistently above $3,000 – it is currently 85% up year on year.

Roche will pay Zymeworks $55 million upfront plus another $40 million once the partnership asset enters Phase 1b development and up to $718 million in additional milestones.
Roche is fronting $55 million for an exclusive global license to Zymeworks’ trispecific T cell engager, which the pharma plans to develop for lung cancer.
On top of its upfront commitment, Roche could be on the hook for $40 million once the asset, dubbed ZW209, starts Phase 1b testing, and up to $718 million in development, commercial and sales milestones. Zymeworks is also entitled to high-single-digit to mid-teen royalties on future net sales, according to a news release Friday morning.
ZW209 is a preclinical trispecific therapy designed to target the DLL3 protein, typically overexpressed on tumor cells. ZW209 also engages CD3 and CD28, both found on T cells, in turn enhancing the immune system’s anti-cancer response. ZW209’s mechanism also avoids the unintended activation of T cells, Zymeworks claims on its website .
“ZW209 represents an innovative approach that complements our ongoing efforts to develop new treatment options for people living with lung cancer,” Boris Zaïtra, head of Corporate Business Development at Roche, said in a prepared statement.
The asset has received the necessary regulatory clearances to start clinical testing and has entered Phase 1a testing, according to the Friday announcement. The study is designed to assess ZW209’s safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics, as well as its early efficacy in patients with advanced solid tumors, such as small cell lung cancer and DLL3-expressing neuroendocrine tumors.
Under the terms of the agreement, Zymeworks will be responsible for running the Phase 1a trial of ZW209 monotherapy in collaboration with Roche, with the pharma providing funding for the study, as per the Friday announcement. Roche will take charge of subsequent global development, regulatory activities and commercialization.
The Roche agreement validates Zymeworks’ royalty-based approach to dealmaking, Leerink Partners said in a Friday morning note. “Monetize internal innovation, shift development costs to partners and retain participation in future commercial upside,” the analysts said, explaining Zymeworks’ model. As an example, they pointed to the biotech’s 2022 partnership with Jazz Pharmaceuticals for the bispecific antibody Ziihera , indicated for gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma and biliary tract cancer.
Zymeworks also has a royalty-driven partnership with Johnson & Johnson, signed in 2017 , for six bispecific antibodies against targets of the pharma’s choosing. In April, Zymeworks lost a colossal collaborator when Bristol Myers Squibb axed the final asset under the legacy alliance between Zymeworks and Celgene. BMS acquired Celgene for $74 billion in 2019.
Friday’s agreement “reinforces our view that ZYME is building a repeatable, diversified business rather than relying on a single asset,” Leerink said.
The Roche deal also comes months after Zymeworks in June acquired Theravance Biopharma for approximately $929 million , gaining the commercial chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder drug Yupelri. Commercialized in the U.S. in partnership with Viatris, Yupelri made $266.6 million in the country last year.
For Roche, Thursday’s partnership with Zymeworks continues a series of deals signed this month, including an antibody-drug conjugate agreement with Hansoh Pharmaceutical worth potentially more than $15 billion, the $1 billion-plus RNA interference gamble with Rona Therapeutics and up to $1.2 billion blood-brain barrier bet with Alector .
